questions.statement: What structure does the second conditional use?
questions.context: In English class at Colegio Anglo Colombiano in Bogotá, the teacher introduces the second conditional.

options.text: If + present simple, will + infinitive
If + past simple, would + infinitive
options.feedback: Correct. The second conditional uses past simple and would.

options.text: If + past perfect, would have + past participle
If + present simple, present simple

questions.explanation:
The second conditional (also called "unreal conditional") is used for hypothetical or unlikely situations in the present or future. The structure is: If + past simple, would + base verb. Example: "If I had a million pesos, I would travel around the world." Note that the past tense does NOT refer to past time here; it expresses unreality.

---

questions.statement: When do we use the third conditional?
questions.context: María is studying the third conditional for her exam at school in Medellín.

options.text: To talk about real facts and general truths.
To talk about possible future situations.
To talk about hypothetical present situations.
To talk about unreal situations in the past and imagine different outcomes.
options.feedback: Correct. The third conditional expresses regret or hypothetical past.

questions.explanation:
The third conditional expresses impossible situations in the past — things that didn't happen. Structure: If + past perfect, would have + past participle. Example: "If I had studied harder, I would have passed the exam." (But I didn't study hard, and I didn't pass.) It is often used to express regret, criticism, or relief about past events.

---

questions.context: Carlos says: "If I were the president, I would improve education." His classmate in Cali asks what this means.

options.text: He is going to be president.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The second conditional expresses an unlikely situation.

options.text: He was president in the past.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Past tense in second conditional does not mean past time.

options.text: He is not the president, so this is a hypothetical/impossible situation in the present.
He will be president in the future.

questions.explanation:
The second conditional uses past tense to talk about present/future situations that are unreal, unlikely, or imaginary. "If I were the president" tells us that the speaker is NOT the president. Note that we use "were" for all subjects (I, he, she, it) in second conditional, not "was" — this is called the subjunctive mood.

questions.statement: What time does the third conditional refer to?
questions.context: Laura reads: "If she had left earlier, she would have caught the bus." She is confused about the time reference.

options.text: The present.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Third conditional is about the past.

options.text: The future.
The past. It means she did NOT leave earlier, so she did NOT catch the bus.
options.feedback: Correct. The third conditional always refers to an unreal past.

options.text: It could be any time.

questions.explanation:
The third conditional always refers to an unreal past situation. "If she had left earlier, she would have caught the bus" implies: She did NOT leave earlier, and she did NOT catch the bus. We use this structure to imagine how things could have been different in the past. It expresses the opposite of what actually happened.

questions.statement: Is Andrés's sentence a second conditional? Why?
questions.context: Andrés is writing a letter to his friend in Barranquilla. He wants to say: "If I had money, I would buy a new phone."

options.text: No, because "had" is past tense.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Second conditional uses past tense.

options.text: Yes, because it talks about a real situation.
Yes, because it uses past simple (had) + would + infinitive (buy) to express an unreal present situation.
options.feedback: Correct. The structure matches the second conditional.

options.text: No, because he doesn't say "if I were."
options.feedback: Incorrect. "If I had" is also correct for second conditional.

questions.explanation:
The sentence "If I had money, I would buy a new phone" is a correct second conditional. It means: I don't have money now (unreal present), so I can't buy a phone. The structure is: If + past simple (had), would + base verb (buy). "If I were" is used with adjectives or nouns ("If I were rich"), but "if I had" is correct for possession.

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly expresses regret about not studying?
questions.context: Santiago wants to express regret about not studying for an exam in Cartagena. Which sentence is correct?

options.text: If I study, I would pass the exam.
If I studied, I would pass the exam.
options.feedback: This is second conditional, refers to present/future, not past regret.

options.text: If I had studied, I would have passed the exam.
options.feedback: Correct. Third conditional expresses past regret.

options.text: If I have studied, I will pass the exam.

questions.explanation:
To express regret about a past action (or inaction), we use the third conditional. "If I had studied" (but I didn't), "I would have passed" (but I didn't). This sentence expresses the speaker's regret about not studying. The second conditional ("If I studied") would be about a hypothetical present situation, not a past one.

questions.statement: What is the difference between S1 (first conditional) and S2 (second conditional)?
questions.context: Valentina is comparing two sentences: S1: "If it rains, I will stay home." S2: "If it rained, I would stay home." She asks about the difference.

options.text: S1 is about the past; S2 is about the present.
There is no difference in meaning.
S1 expresses a real possibility (it might rain); S2 expresses an unlikely or imaginary situation.
options.feedback: Correct. First conditional is possible; second is hypothetical.

options.text: S1 is grammatically incorrect.

questions.explanation:
The first conditional (if + present, will) expresses a real possibility: "If it rains" means it might actually rain. The second conditional (if + past, would) expresses an unlikely or hypothetical situation: "If it rained" suggests that rain is unlikely or imaginary. The choice of conditional changes the likelihood the speaker assigns to the condition.

questions.statement: What does this sentence tell us about what actually happened?
questions.context: Camila reads: "If I had known about the party, I would have gone." She analyzes the meaning.

options.text: She knew about the party and she went.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "If I had known" implies she didn't know.

options.text: She did NOT know about the party, and she did NOT go.
options.feedback: Correct. The third conditional expresses the opposite of reality.

options.text: She knew about the party but she didn't go.
options.feedback: Incorrect. The condition is about knowing, not about going.

options.text: She didn't know but she went anyway.

questions.explanation:
The third conditional expresses the opposite of what happened. "If I had known" → She did NOT know. "I would have gone" → She did NOT go. Reality: She didn't know, and she didn't go. This is why the third conditional is called "past unreal" — it describes a past situation that is contrary to fact.

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly uses "were" in a second conditional?
questions.context: Sebastián needs to write a sentence using "were" (not "was") in a second conditional for his class in Bucaramanga.

options.text: If I was you, I would study more.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "If I were you" is the correct form.

options.text: If I were you, I would study more.
options.feedback: Correct. "If I were" is the subjunctive form.

options.text: If I were study, I would pass.
options.feedback: Incorrect. "Were" is not followed by a base verb.

options.text: If I was been you, I would study.

questions.explanation:
In the second conditional, the correct form is "if I were" (subjunctive mood), not "if I was." Example: "If I were you, I would accept the offer." This is true for all subjects: if I were, if he were, if she were, if it were. "If I were you" is a very common fixed expression used to give advice.

---

questions.statement: What is special about this mixed conditional?
questions.context: Isabella finds a mixed conditional: "If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now."

options.text: It is incorrect; both parts must be the same type.
It is a normal second conditional.
It is a normal third conditional.
It mixes third conditional (if clause about past) with second conditional (result about present).
options.feedback: Correct. The if clause refers to an unreal past, the result to the present.

questions.explanation:
Mixed conditionals combine different time references. Here, "if I had studied medicine" (past unreal — I didn't study) is the third conditional if-clause, and "I would be a doctor now" (present unreal — I'm not a doctor) is the second conditional result clause. This is common when a past action (or inaction) has a present result.

---

questions.statement: Is "If she would have studied, she would have passed" correct?
questions.context: Daniel is editing a text and finds: "If she would have studied, she would have passed." He thinks it might be wrong.

options.text: Yes, it is perfectly correct.
No, but it's acceptable in formal writing.
No, the correct form is "If she had studied, she would have passed" (no "would" in the if-clause).
options.feedback: Correct. "Would" should not be in the if-clause.

options.text: Yes, because both clauses need "would".
options.feedback: Incorrect. Only the result clause uses "would."

questions.explanation:
A common error is putting "would" in the if-clause. The correct structure is: If + past perfect (had studied), would have + past participle (would have passed). "Would" should only appear in the result clause, not the if-clause. This is a grammar rule for all conditional sentences.

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly uses a modal other than "would" in a conditional?
questions.context: In class at the school in Sincelejo, the teacher asks: "Can we use 'could' or 'might' instead of 'would' in conditionals?"

options.text: If I had more time, I could help you.
options.feedback: Correct. "Could" can replace "would" in second conditional.

options.text: If I have money, I could buy it.
options.feedback: Incorrect. First conditional uses "will" or modals with present tense.

options.text: If I had studied, I could passed.
Both A and C are correct.

questions.explanation:
In conditional sentences, we can use "could" (ability/possibility) or "might" (probability) instead of "would" in the result clause. For second conditional: "If I had more time, I could help you" (ability) or "If I saved money, I might buy a car" (possibility). For third conditional: "If I had studied, I could have passed" or "I might have passed."
